intro: Fencing is combat with blades on a long, narrow strip called the piste. Electronic scoring registers each hit (a 'touch'), but the three weapons — foil, épée and sabre — have their own target areas and, crucially, their own logic for who scores when both fencers hit at once. The Fédération Internationale d'Escrime (FIE) publishes the rules.
inThirtySeconds: Hit your opponent's valid target with your weapon before they hit you.
Foil and sabre use 'right of way': the fencer who attacked first gets the point.
In épée, the whole body is target and simultaneous hits score for both.
Elimination bouts go to 15 touches, in three periods of three minutes.
objective: Reach the required number of touches first (15 in direct elimination), or lead when time expires.

scoring.label: Touch
scoring.detail: A valid hit on the target area registered by the scoring apparatus.

scoring.label: Double touch
scoring.detail: In épée only, both fencers score if they hit within a fraction of a second.

scoring.label: Bout
scoring.detail: Direct-elimination bouts are won by the first to 15 touches.

variants.name: Foil
variants.description: Thrusting weapon; target is the torso. Right of way applies.

variants.name: Épée
variants.description: Thrusting weapon; the whole body is target and there is no right of way.

variants.name: Sabre
variants.description: Cutting and thrusting weapon; target is everything above the waist. Right of way applies.

chapters.title: Weapons and targets
chapters.summary: Each weapon has its own target and way of hitting.

rules.title: Foil: the torso
rules.summary: Only hits with the point on the torso (front and back) count. Arms, legs and most of the head are off-target.
rules.body: An off-target hit lights a white lamp and stops the action, but no touch is awarded. The target is covered by a conductive jacket (lamé) so valid hits light a coloured lamp.

rules.title: Épée: the whole body
rules.summary: Hits with the point anywhere on the body, from mask to foot, are valid.
rules.body: There is no right of way. If both fencers hit within the machine's lockout time (a fraction of a second), both score a touch.
rules.example: Both fencers land at almost the same instant — one on the hand, one on the foot: double touch, one point each.

rules.title: Sabre: above the waist
rules.summary: Hits with the edge or point anywhere above the waist — including head and arms, but not the hands — are valid.
rules.body: Sabre is the fastest weapon. Fencers may not cross their feet when advancing, which rules out the running 'flèche' attack used in the other weapons.

chapters.title: Right of way
chapters.summary: Who scores when both lights go on.

rules.title: Priority to the attacker
rules.summary: When both fencers hit, the touch goes to the one who established the attack first.
rules.body: An attack is the first offensive action made by extending the arm and threatening the target. The defender gains priority by parrying (deflecting the blade) and then hitting back — the riposte. If the attacker misses or is parried, priority switches. The referee analyses each phrase and explains the decision with hand signals.
rules.example: Fencer A lunges with the arm extended; fencer B hits at the same time without parrying: point to A.

rules.title: Leaving the piste
rules.summary: Stepping off the back of the piste with both feet gives a touch to the opponent; stepping off the side leads to a penalty of ground.
rules.body: The piste is about 14 m long and 1.5–2 m wide. Warning lines near each end tell fencers they are close to the rear limit.

rules.title: Yellow, red and black cards
rules.summary: Infringements are punished with a yellow card (warning), red card (a touch to the opponent) or black card (exclusion).
rules.body: Typical offences include covering the target, turning the back, corps-à-corps in foil and sabre, or disrupting order. Non-combativity — a long period without fencing — can also be penalised.

fouls.name: Covering the target
fouls.description: Using the free arm or another body part to protect the valid target.

fouls.name: Corps-à-corps
fouls.description: Body contact in foil or sabre.

fouls.name: Crossing the rear limit
fouls.description: Both feet over the end line.

flow.title: Salute
flow.description: Fencers salute each other and the referee before putting on masks.

flow.title: En garde, prêts, allez
flow.description: The referee starts each action from the en-garde lines.

flow.title: Halt and decision
flow.description: After each hit, the referee stops play and awards the touch.

flow.title: Handshake
flow.description: Fencers remove masks and shake hands at the end — failing to do so is penalised.

positions.name: Fencer on the right
positions.role: Wears the green light on the scoring box.

positions.name: Fencer on the left
positions.role: Wears the red light on the scoring box.

positions.name: Referee (president)
positions.role: Starts and stops the action and awards touches.

field.name: Piste
field.dimensions: About 14 m long × 1.5–2 m wide, with run-off at each end
notes: Centre line, en-garde lines 2 m from it
Warning zones before each rear limit

glossary.definition: The counter-attack after a successful parry.
A running attack, banned in sabre.

funFacts: Fencing has featured at every modern Olympic Games since 1896.
Electric scoring arrived in épée in the 1930s, foil in the 1950s and sabre only in 1988.
